### TAG-196: Unit Cube Geometry

**Status:** ✅ Implemented

## Software Notes

My suggestion: use something small, boring-in-a-good-way, and trivially self-checking as the flagship first example — a **cube**. It's the natural next step up from the unit-square example already sitting in the doc (extrude it): 8 points, 12 edges, 6 loops, 6 faces, every seam goes the same direction (no reversal trick needed anywhere), and anyone glancing at the render can instantly tell if it's a cube or not. It still exercises the full pipeline end-to-end — points → edges → loops → faces → `resolveSpatialBindings` → `triangulate` → `exportPly` → an actual printable `.ply` — which is really the thing worth demonstrating for a first example, not shape complexity.

None of the Möbius work is wasted, to be clear — `spatial_domain.zig`, the `mesh.zig` export module, and the loop-closure validation are all shape-agnostic; only the demo file itself changes. I'd suggest keeping `mobius_strip.ms.ipl` around as a **second, "advanced topology" example** further down the doc, once the basics are established and (per your point last message) once there's a way to actually verify face winding/normals rather than eyeballing a shaded render — at that point it becomes a genuinely good showcase of capability rather than a confusing first impression.

## Reference

```
cube[()()
    @domain(spatial3d)

    // 8 corners: b0..b3 form the bottom face (z=0),
    // t0..t3 form the top face (z=1), directly above
    // their b-counterparts.
    p0< point(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) >  // b0
    p1< point(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) >  // b1
    p2< point(1.0, 1.0, 0.0) >  // b2
    p3< point(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) >  // b3
    p4< point(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) >  // t0
    p5< point(1.0, 0.0, 1.0) >  // t1
    p6< point(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) >  // t2
    p7< point(0.0, 1.0, 1.0) >  // t3

    // Each of the 6 faces owns its own 4 edges, even where an
    // edge geometrically coincides with one used by a neighboring
    // face (e.g. p0->p1 appears both here and in the front face).
    // This keeps every loop closing in a single consistent
    // direction with no reversed-edge traversal needed anywhere —
    // unlike the Möbius example, an ordinary cube's faces never
    // need to share a directed edge to stay correct.

    // bottom face: b0 -> b1 -> b2 -> b3 -> b0
    e_b0<edge($p0, $p1)>
    e_b1<edge($p1, $p2)>
    e_b2<edge($p2, $p3)>
    e_b3<edge($p3, $p0)>
    l_bottom<loop($e_b0, $e_b1, $e_b2, $e_b3)>
    f_bottom<face($l_bottom)>

    // top face: t0 -> t1 -> t2 -> t3 -> t0
    e_t0<edge($p4, $p5)>
    e_t1<edge($p5, $p6)>
    e_t2<edge($p6, $p7)>
    e_t3<edge($p7, $p4)>
    l_top<loop($e_t0, $e_t1, $e_t2, $e_t3)>
    f_top<face($l_top)>

    // front face: b0 -> b1 -> t1 -> t0 -> b0
    e_f0<edge($p0, $p1)>
    e_f1<edge($p1, $p5)>
    e_f2<edge($p5, $p4)>
    e_f3<edge($p4, $p0)>
    l_front<loop($e_f0, $e_f1, $e_f2, $e_f3)>
    f_front<face($l_front)>

    // right face: b1 -> b2 -> t2 -> t1 -> b1
    e_r0<edge($p1, $p2)>
    e_r1<edge($p2, $p6)>
    e_r2<edge($p6, $p5)>
    e_r3<edge($p5, $p1)>
    l_right<loop($e_r0, $e_r1, $e_r2, $e_r3)>
    f_right<face($l_right)>

    // back face: b2 -> b3 -> t3 -> t2 -> b2
    e_k0<edge($p2, $p3)>
    e_k1<edge($p3, $p7)>
    e_k2<edge($p7, $p6)>
    e_k3<edge($p6, $p2)>
    l_back<loop($e_k0, $e_k1, $e_k2, $e_k3)>
    f_back<face($l_back)>

    // left face: b3 -> b0 -> t0 -> t3 -> b3
    e_l0<edge($p3, $p0)>
    e_l1<edge($p0, $p4)>
    e_l2<edge($p4, $p7)>
    e_l3<edge($p7, $p3)>
    l_left<loop($e_l0, $e_l1, $e_l2, $e_l3)>
    f_left<face($l_left)>
    :
]
```
